cards.title: Neat liquid phosphoric acid (H 3 PO 4 ) has the highest intrinsic proton conductivity of any known substance and is a useful model for understanding proton transport in other phosphate-based systems in biology and clean energy technologies. Here, we present an  ab initio  molecular dynamics study that reveals, for the first time, the microscopic mechanism of this high proton conductivity. Anomalously fast proton transport in hydrogen-bonded systems involves a structural diffusion mechanism in which intramolecular proton transfer is driven by specific hydrogen bond rearrangements in the surrounding environment. Aqueous media transport excess charge defects through local hydrogen bond rearrangements that drive individual proton transfer reactions. In contrast, strong, polarizable hydrogen bonds in phosphoric acid produce coupled proton motion and a pronounced protic dielectric response of the medium, leading to the formation of extended, polarized hydrogen-bonded chains. The interplay between these chains and a frustrated hydrogen-bond network gives rise to the high proton conductivity. U
cards.summary: Anomalously fast proton transport in hydrogen-bonded systems involves a structural diffusion mechanism driven by specific hydrogen bond rearrangements. Strong, polarizable hydrogen bonds in phosphoric acid produce coupled proton motion and a pronounced protic dielectric response. The high proton conductivity arises from the interplay between extended, polarized hydrogen-bonded chains and a frustrated hydrogen-bond network.

synthesis_notes:
## Literature Evidence Context (s05)

Context for s05: 7 mechanism claims, 3 measurements

- [manual_15d8390320|mechanism_claim] Proton shuttling through the frozen water wire predominantly occurs via Grotthuss diffusion.
- [manual_15d8390320|mechanism_claim] In the CNT (6,6) nanopore, Grotthuss diffusion plays a dominant role, while in the CNT (7,7) nanopore, it is primarily just rattling within the Zundel cation.
- [manual_3e0fc6547f|mechanism_claim] The proton transport relies on the Grotthuss mechanism characterized by ordered hydrogen-bonded chains.
- [manual_8beb2711e9|mechanism_claim] Protons migrate along oxygen sites in the ZrO6 octahedra through the Grotthuss (hopping) mechanism.
- [manual_8beb2711e9|mechanism_claim] Thermal activation drives the proton hopping from one oxygen to another by overcoming an energy barrier.
- [manual_e2d21540be|mechanism_claim] There are two principal mechanisms recognized for proton transport in liquids: the vehicle mechanism and the Grotthuss mechanism.
- [manual_e2d21540be|mechanism_claim] Proton migration in phosphoric acid is thought to be achieved through the Grotthuss mechanism, characterized by local proton hopping within hydrogen bonds.
- [manual_15d8390320|direct_measurement] water density increase = 40 % (in CNT (7,7) nanopore with hydrated excess proton)
- [manual_15d8390320|direct_measurement] water density increase = 20 % (in CNT (7,7) nanopore with K+)
- [manual_3e0fc6547f|direct_measurement] proton conductivity enhancement = up to 500 times (in the polymer-to-MOF direction compared to the opposite direction)

Across the cards, the strongest consistent constraint is that nanoscale confinement can impose highly ordered/“frozen” hydrogen-bond networks that favor structural (Grotthuss) proton diffusion over vehicular motion, with transport properties changing sharply with confinement length scale/diameter (CNT 0.81 vs 0.95 nm; heterostructured nanochannels with confined water clusters). This broadly supports mechanisms built on confined acid–water networks enabling hopping (H1) and is compatible with interfacial/surface-templated hopping in nanochannels or mineral pores (H3), but by itself does not establish VTF-governed relaxation or percolation behavior. Evidence for hydration-dependent regime changes is clearest in phosphoric-acid/water mixtures where structural diffusion shows a non-monotonic maximum with water content and can largely vanish at specific hydrates (e.g., H3PO4·2H2O), implying a crossover between proton-transport “populations” or mechanisms as bound vs freer water changes (supporting the spirit of H2). Polymer acid-doping studies (H3PO4-doped PBI) reinforce that conductivity is strongly controlled by acid loading and humidity and can be enhanced by inorganic fillers, which is consistent with a composite/interfacial pathway picture (H3) and with loading-controlled connectivity effects (directionally supportive of H4, though not definitive on percolation thresholds). The Meyer–Neldel/anti–Meyer–Neldel observations and isokinetic-temperature framing indicate compensation behavior in ionic conductors (activation–prefactor correlations) that could be consistent with changing segmental/relaxation-limited transport descriptions often associated with VTF-like phenomenology (weakly supporting H1/H4), but these cards do not uniquely tie compensation to a specific confined-acid percolation mechanism. The acid-in-clay electrolyte result directly anchors the relevance of a natural clay network hosting fast proton carriers and achieving substantial conductivity over temperature, lending concrete plausibility to clay-mediated/interfacial conduction (H3) and to connectivity/loading control (H4), while freeze–thaw salt-trapping and generic Li-ion nanoconfinement effects are largely orthogonal and do not discriminate among proton-specific hypotheses.
